findings.subject: /tmp
findings.detail: /tmp is not a separate mount: it is part of the filesystem mounted at / and inherits its options. nodev, nosuid and noexec are per-mount properties, so a directory that is merely a subdirectory of another filesystem cannot carry them — and /tmp is where anything an unprivileged account brings to the host lands, so it is the one filesystem where removing the ability to execute, to escalate through setuid and to reach a device is worth the inconvenience

findings.subject: /home

findings.subject: sysctl configuration
findings.detail: Reverse-path filtering is written to the sysctl configuration: net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter is 2 at /etc/sysctl.d/10-network-security.conf:5; net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter is 2 at /etc/sysctl.d/10-network-security.conf:4. The floor is set for the interfaces already up and the template for every interface created after boot, so a spoofed source address is dropped after the next reboot either way. net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter, net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter are at 2, which is loose mode: the source has to be routable by some interface rather than by the one the packet arrived on. That is the right choice on a multi-homed host with asymmetric routing and the wrong one on a host with a single default route, where strict mode costs nothing. This reads the sysctl configuration files, which describe what the kernel will do after the next reboot; what it is doing now is KERNEL-0008's subject, and a disagreement between the two is KERNEL-0007's.

findings.subject: sysctl configuration
findings.detail: net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route is not set in any sysctl configuration file, so nothing on this host records that source-routed packets should be dropped; the kernel's own default is 0, which is correct and is not a decision anybody made; net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route is not set in any sysctl configuration file, so an interface created after boot — a container veth, a VPN tunnel, a hot-plugged NIC — inherits whatever the kernel defaults to rather than a value this host chose; net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects is not set in any sysctl configuration file, so this host will accept ICMP redirects, because unlike source routing the kernel defaults this one to 1: any party on the segment can rewrite its routing table with an unauthenticated packet; net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects is not set in any sysctl configuration file, so every interface created after boot will accept ICMP redirects, since the kernel defaults this one to 1 and nothing here overrides it. Both parameters let a party on the network decide where this host sends packets, which is a position to read and rewrite traffic from rather than a weakness in it. This reads the sysctl configuration files, which describe what the kernel will do after the next reboot. What it is doing now is KERNEL-0015's subject for source routing and nothing's yet for redirect acceptance, and a disagreement between file and kernel is KERNEL-0007's.

findings.detail: All 70 enablement symlinks resolve to a unit file that exists, so every service an administrator enabled on this host has something for systemd to start.
All 18 unit directories and 240 unit files are owned by root and writable by root alone, so nothing but root decides what starts at boot.

1 of the 2 audited services installed here sets NoNewPrivileges: systemd-journald.service. A compromise of it cannot gain privileges through a setuid binary or file capabilities. Not held to this standard: cron.service (runs user cron jobs in its own process tree, and no_new_privs is inherited by every child — so a job that calls sudo, su, or any setuid binary stops working, and fails at the job rather than at the restart). An exemption is a documented reason the setting would break the service, not a finding that was suppressed. This examines NoNewPrivileges on a fixed list of units and says nothing about the other services on this host, nor about the other sandboxing directives on these ones.

evidence.excerpt: cron.service: NoNewPrivileges not set; the default is off
systemd-journald.service: NoNewPrivileges=yes

findings.subject: /usr/lib/systemd/system/systemd-journald.service
findings.detail: systemd-journald.service leaves the system directories writable, so a compromise of it can replace a binary under /usr or a boot loader file and survive the service being restarted. Not held to this standard: cron.service (runs arbitrary operator-supplied jobs inside its own mount namespace, so a read-only /usr or /etc becomes a restriction on code the packager never saw — a job that updates a package or rewrites a config file fails, and fails at the job rather than at the restart). An exemption is a documented reason the setting would break the service, not a finding that was suppressed. This examines ProtectSystem on a fixed list of units. It says nothing about the other services on this host, nor about the other sandboxing directives on these ones, nor about what a ReadWritePaths= may have opened up again.

evidence.excerpt: systemd-journald.service: ProtectSystem not set; the default is no

findings.subject: /usr/lib/systemd/system/systemd-journald.service
findings.detail: systemd-journald.service can reach /home, /root and /run/user, so a compromise of it can read an SSH private key, a cloud credential file or a cached token belonging to any user on this host and reuse it elsewhere. Not held to this standard: cron.service (runs arbitrary operator-supplied jobs inside its own mount namespace, and user cron jobs routinely execute scripts kept in a home directory and read data from one — so the jobs fail, and fail at the job rather than at the restart). An exemption is a documented reason the setting would break the service, not a finding that was suppressed. This examines ProtectHome on a fixed list of units. It says nothing about the other services on this host, nor about the other sandboxing directives on these ones, nor about what a ReadWritePaths= or a BindPaths= may have opened up again.

evidence.excerpt: systemd-journald.service: ProtectHome not set; the default is no
